item.title: Directed brain-body graphs across timescales
item.description: arXiv:2611.31440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simultaneous brain and body recordings combine signals sampled at very different rates with processes that act on timescales from milliseconds to minutes. Placing all signals on one time grid can distort the directed relationships estimated from them. Unmeasured common influences can also make one signal appear to drive another. We introduce rate-matched Granger causality (RMGC), which estimates directed predictive relationships without a common sampling grid. Each relationship receives a robustness value, the strength of the weakest common influence found within a specified class that can reproduce it. A neural extension tests for nonlinear relationships. In a controlled benchmark, RMGC recovered more true relationships than four established methods and an autoregressive model on a common grid (92\% at a false-positive rate of 5\%). Given the same signal features, the common-grid model matched this recovery but had more than twice the false-positive rate, and it reversed the relationship from respiration to heart rate. The robustness value never overstated the strength of the driver behind a spurious relationship, even for drivers outside the searched class. It separated true from spurious relationships better than predictive strength did. In overnight sleep recordings and two awake datasets, many brain--heart relationships could be reproduced by common drivers no stronger than measured respiration. Robustness values only partly identified those that appeared when respiration was omitted, particularly during wakefulness. Surrogate analyses showed elevated background rates in one awake dataset. The approach applies to other signals recorded at different rates or as events, provided that influences act with a delay.
item.dc:creator: Lu\'is A. Alexandre, Karolina Finc

item.title: Neural-operator acceleration of bidirectional phonon Boltzmann-Fourier coupling for multiscale heat transport in silicon fin arrays
item.description: arXiv:2611.31542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Localized heating in semiconductor devices can produce non-diffusive phonon transport near heat-generating regions, while heat spreading through the surrounding substrate remains well described by Fourier conduction. We present a hybrid framework that couples a pretrained neural operator for the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) within individual fins to a Fourier model of a shared substrate. To reduce the cost of repeated BTE solves across fin positions and coupling iterations, a DeepONet maps each fin's substrate-interface temperature and heating state to its temperature and heat-flux fields. The operator is trained on interface temperatures generated by a linearized proxy of the coupled problem, which avoids explicit training data collection from full coupled runs. An energy-balance penalty regularizes the learned operator, and a mixed finite-element formulation represents substrate heat flux in an H(div)-conforming space. The two models exchange temperature and normal heat flux through a non-overlapping Schwarz iteration with adaptive Aitken relaxation. We evaluate the framework on an idealized three-dimensional array of 100 silicon fins. For a held-out switching configuration, the neural-operator-Fourier solution differs from the direct BTE-Fourier reference by a maximum of 0.3 K in temperature and 0.6% in relative flux across all fins. Excluding the one-time substrate factorization, the coupled surrogate run takes about 50 s, compared with 2 h 28 min for direct coupling, a speedup of approximately 180x. Additional held-out switching patterns converge with the same trained operator. These results demonstrate neural-operator acceleration of bidirectional kinetic-continuum coupling for the tested geometry and material. This bidirectional strategy may extend to other multiscale materials problems coupling learned local neural models with continuum solvers.
item.dc:creator: Ruthwik Chivukula, Khemraj Shukla, George Em Karniadakis

item.title: How problem formulation shapes simulation-based optimisation of tracked vehicle suspension
item.description: arXiv:2611.31592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulation-based optimisation is an established tool for vehicle suspension design, but how the optimisation problem should be formulated has received little attention. This paper investigates how the choice of objectives, evaluation scenarios and constraints influences the resulting design. A multibody model of a tracked vehicle with parameterised torsion-rod suspension and semi-active damping is combined with Bayesian optimisation to evaluate designs over representative terrain. Three formulations are investigated, progressing from single-objective ride-quality optimisation to a constrained multi-objective formulation balancing rough-terrain speed against pitch comfort on easy roads. The two single-objective formulations give similar designs that neglect comfort in routine driving, while the multi-objective formulation spans a trade-off from a middle-weighted, lightly damped comfort design to a forward-supported, more strongly damped performance design. The results demonstrate that problem formulation is a key component of simulation-based suspension design and should be considered as carefully as the suspension model itself.
item.dc:creator: Markus Pogulis, Martin Servin

item.title: Stopping criteria in structural reliability analysis: An overview
item.description: arXiv:2611.31706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stopping criteria have become a crucial component of probabilistic and statistical methods in structural reliability analysis, helping prevent structural defects and failures, as well as inaccurate evaluations of existing structures. Over time, these rules have evolved in both concept and application, whereas their treatment in the literature remains fragmented. They are often developed and presented in connection with specific models or analytical frameworks, obscuring their broader applicability across diverse models and methodologies. On this basis, the aim of this article is twofold. First, it overviews a wide range of stopping rules, drawing on concepts from applied probability and statistics. These strategies include classical methods based on error estimates or variance, and stability detection. While many of these ideas were developed in other fields, they have the potential to offer useful tools for structural reliability tasks like managing sampling, improving surrogate models, and checking for convergence. Second, this article introduces a structured framework to organize past and recent developments in this area. It brings together various stopping criteria, clarifies their conceptual roles, explains their theoretical foundations, and compares their practical strengths and limitations. By relating these methods to common modeling and methodological practices, and by incorporating a systematic comparison of performance aspects such as accuracy, computational cost, and robustness, we aim to identify dominant strategies, highlight shared challenges, and point to directions for further progress.
item.dc:creator: Reiichiro Kawai

item.title: topAC99: A compact MATLAB implementation of filter-free Allen--Cahn topology optimization with matrix-free field transfer
item.description: arXiv:2611.31885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents topAC99, a self-contained, toolbox-free 99-line MATLAB kernel for filter-free Allen--Cahn topology optimization via the Augmented Lagrangian method on structured quadrilateral meshes. The software architecture combines three compact numerical components: (i) a lumped nodal discretization with a 7-line Kronecker-sum 5-point Laplacian that enforces homogeneous Neumann conditions at width-invariant sparse memory cost; (ii) matrix-free node-to-element averaging and adjoint backpropagation via two-dimensional convolutions (conv2); and (iii) an inlined 18-line 1D-dual bisection Method of Moving Asymptotes (MMA) solver for signed sensitivities. Benchmarks from 60x40 to 300x200 meshes (121,002 degrees of freedom) against convolution- and PDE-filtered SIMP baselines show that Allen--Cahn residual and adjoint evaluations add only 0.7%--1.2% per-step overhead while converging in 78--92 iterations on fine grids. Minimal-line extensions to a symmetric force inverter compliant mechanism and a passive-deck highway arch bridge further demonstrate the versatility of the 99-line kernel.
item.dc:creator: Run Du

item.title: Learning Inelastic Homogenization with Memory: Deep Material Networks and Discrete Adjoints
item.description: arXiv:2611.32499v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep material networks (DMNs) provide mechanically structured surrogate models for computational homogenization. Traditionally, they are identified from elastic data and subsequently extrapolated to inelastic responses. This procedure leverages highly efficient linear solvers and provides robust extrapolation to different inelastic constitutive laws. However, selecting the appropriate linear elastic training data for a given inelastic constitutive behavior is non-trivial. In this work, we identify the DMNs directly from macroscopic stress-strain trajectories. Applying automatic differentiation to such problems with history entails a huge memory demand, excluding most practically relevant problems. To mitigate, we derive a path-consistent discrete adjoint that avoids propagating parameter-wise state sensitivities by treating equilibrium and internal variable evolution over the complete loading history as coupled constraints. For a short-fiber composite with an elastoplastic matrix, the adjoint approach reproduces the sensitivities obtained by direct differentiation and by an independent automatic-differentiation implementation, while it requires only one backward solve of the linearized state equations per time step and avoids the parameter-wise propagation of state sensitivities. Inelastic training also improves predictive accuracy: A rank-$5$ DMN trained on inelastic trajectories outperforms a deeper rank-$8$ DMN trained on elastic homogenization data for different loading paths. This advantage is retained under perturbations of the constituent inelastic material parameters. The resulting inelastic trained DMNs preserve the same formulation for online deployment and remain several orders of magnitude faster than the full-field homogenization solver.
item.dc:creator: Binh Huy Nguyen, Matti Schneider

item.title: Low-Frequency Stable Single-Source Integral Equation
item.description: arXiv:2611.32561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Among the integral equations for scattering by homogeneous dielectric objects, single-source integral equations (SSIEs) provide the advantage of having only a single electric or magnetic current unknown. A well-conditioned SSIE can be obtained by appropriately combining the interior and exterior Calder\'on formulas. The condition number of the resulting operator appearing in the well-conditioned SSIE remains bounded at low frequencies. However, SSIEs still suffer from low-frequency cancellation, causing loss of significant digits in the solution, the right-hand side, and the system matrix. In this work, we apply a rescaling strategy based on quasi-Helmholtz projectors to the well-conditioned SSIE. Primal and dual space projectors are required since both primal and dual spaces are used to discretize the SSIE operators. We show that the solution of the rescaled SSIE is immune to catastrophic cancellations at low frequencies. Numerical experiments corroborate the method by testing the accuracy of the radiated field for extremely low frequencies.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Zuccotti, Cedric M\"unger, Chien V. Le, Paul Olyslager, Kristof Cools

item.title: Accuracy and Efficiency of Lowest-order and Higher-Order Single-Source Integral Equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.32608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The single-source integral equation allows the modeling of the electromagnetic field by only tracking a single surface-supported current density. It features products of integral operators, which pose unique challenges for the modeler in both the discretization and solution of the equation. Due to the unique structure of the single-source equation, its conforming and stable discretization requires expanding one of the two physical traces in primal basis functions and the other in dual basis functions. Primal functions are expected to have better approximation properties than dual ones. In this work, we study the impact of this asymmetric representation on the accuracy of the solution and propose an approach from which both traces can be recovered using only primal functions with modest additional computational cost. Moreover, we propose an alternative discretization scheme based on approximating the inverse of the duality mapping induced by the surface normal cross-product operator through the quasi-Helmholtz decomposition. This discretization provides greater flexibility in the choice of function spaces, enabling both a higher-order extension of the single-source equation and a more efficient lowest-order discretization using only Rao-Wilton-Glisson basis functions. Numerical results show the impact of the representation in terms of primal and dual functions in both lowest- and higher-order discretization.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Zuccotti, Cedric M\"unger, Kristof Cools

item.title: DED-Agent: An agentic AI method for autonomous thermal simulation model development and calibration in laser directed energy deposition
item.description: arXiv:2611.32822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In metal additive manufacturing (AM), process parameters set the local thermal history, which governs defects, microstructure and properties. Laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, scan strategy and position combine into a design space of 10^4-10^6 conditions, which is beyond what human experts can map by hand with finite element (FE) thermal models: every model must be set up, meshed, solved and calibrated by an expert, and calibrating unknown heat-source parameters alone can take days to weeks. This paper presents DED-Agent, an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) method for autonomous simulation model development and calibration in laser directed energy deposition (L-DED). A supervisor agent coordinates three specialist agents that share a structured simulation specification and call open-source tools. An intent agent turns a plain-language request into a validated specification, a simulation agent builds, runs and checks an FE thermal model through physics-aware step-by-step reasoning, and a calibration agent identifies key heat-source parameters against experimental data (e.g., thermocouple data) using a high-order proper generalized decomposition (HOPGD) surrogate within a trust-region search. On five benchmark builds, from single-track walls to a multi-track band on a cylindrical tube, the agents built executable thermal models without manual intervention, with 4.1-9.1% error for the simple and medium builds. Within three calibration rounds, the error fell to 0.9-2.5%. The surrogate matched full FE to within 0.08-1.55% and shortened calibration by 5-13 times. Agentic AI can thus autonomously establish reliable, accurate simulation models for AM processes and accelerate the search for process parameters that control microstructure.
item.dc:creator: Michael Song, Yilong Dai, Lin Cheng

item.title: Automated classification of modal displacements
item.description: arXiv:2611.31472v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The bending, torsional, or coupled character of a mode shape helps determine the dynamic behaviour of aerospace and civil structures. In vibration testing, it is assigned by inspecting mode shape plots, and depends on the analyst. This work proposes four indices to describe the motion of a mode from a few sensor vectors: a bending score, a torsion score, a twist share and an in-plane ratio. They are assessed on the first eight finite element modes of a tapered plate with a swept trailing edge. They are applied to identified XB-2 wing modes and to the published modes of the Sheraton Universal Hotel, a reinforced concrete (RC) building. On the plate, the twist share separates bending, coupled and torsion modes. The XB-2 modes include one bending and three coupled modes (one dominated by in-plane bending and two by out-of-plane bending). The coupled mode dominated by in-plane bending (15.25 Hz, in-plane ratio 1.33) was not investigated in earlier campaigns on the wing. On the RC building, all five modes are bending (twist share below 0.0005). The twist share and the in-plane ratio indicate the type of each mode. Hence, modes are classified without visually inspecting the mode shapes. Code and processed data are openly released.
item.dc:creator: Gabriele Dessena, Marco Civera, Saray Undiano Ech\'aniz, Oscar Bonilla-Manrique

item.title: Boundary Representation-Driven Graph Transformer Modeling for Machining Operation Sequencing
item.description: arXiv:2611.31661v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machining process planning is inherently complex due to the interdependence between part geometry, machining operations, and evolving manufacturable states. Traditional approaches rely heavily on expert knowledge and rule-based systems, limiting scalability and automation. While recent machine learning methods have shown promise, most operate on simplified geometric representations, such as voxels or hand-crafted features, which fail to fully exploit the rich geometric and topological information encoded in Boundary Representation (B-Rep) models. In this work, we propose a graph transformer-based framework for geometry-to-sequence learning that directly predicts machining operation sequences from B-Rep design geometry. The proposed method constructs topology-aware graphs from B-Rep entities, where faces and their adjacencies are encoded as node and edge features capturing both geometric and relational information. A graph neural network encoder learns geometry-aware embeddings, which are then used to condition a dual-decoder transformer that autoregressively generates machining operation sequences. This formulation enables the model to capture both operation-type prediction and process-level ordering constraints directly from design geometry, without requiring intermediate feature extraction or machining-state representations. Experiments on a dataset of 2,991 synthetic machined parts demonstrate strong performance, achieving 95% accuracy for main operation prediction, 64% accuracy for sub-operation prediction, and 93% accuracy for sequence length prediction. Further analysis shows that the model effectively captures precedence relationships and geometry-dependent constraints inherent in machining processes. These results highlight the potential of B-Rep-driven graph learning for scalable and automated machining process planning.
item.dc:creator: Fatemeh Elhambakhsh, Gaurav Ameta, Aditi Roy, Hyunwoong Ko

item.title: Large-Scale Streaming Portfolio Optimization with Pauli Correlation Encoding
item.description: arXiv:2611.32769v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Classical portfolio construction over large asset universes is a combinatorial selection problem that existing heuristics do not solve well at scale. Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) addresses this by representing the underlying clustering problem with far fewer qubits than one per asset, and a prior study showed it is competitive with classical methods on a single historical snapshot. This paper moves beyond that static test to a streaming deployment, in which the correlation structure and the portfolio are both re-estimated on a rolling basis, as a live rebalancing system would actually operate. We introduce two streaming variants -- PCE itself and a joint multi-cut variant, dPCE -- and evaluate both against a Buy & Hold baseline across window lengths, portfolio sizes up to several thousand assets, risk-aversion and transaction-cost settings, and measurement-shot budgets. Streaming PCE and dPCE consistently outperform the passive baseline, including during a market downturn where both lose money but PCE loses markedly less -- evidence that the method's value is not confined to rising markets. PCE also proves the more practical choice at scale, since dPCE's resource requirements and its sensitivity to rebalancing frequency both grow faster with portfolio size. We further report which operational choices -- rebalancing cadence, shot budget, and transaction-cost awareness -- matter most for a real deployment, and which matter less than commonly assumed.
item.dc:creator: Vicente P. Soloviev, Josh Kirsopp

item.title: Quantum-Inspired Tensor Train Spectral Solver for High-Resolution PDEs with Non-Periodic Boundary Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2611.32968v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tensor train (TT) methods enable high-resolution computational mechanics simulations by exploiting low-rank structure in discretized fields and operators. While the superfast Fourier transform (SFFT) has enabled efficient TT-based spectral solvers for periodic problems, corresponding representations for non-periodic boundary conditions remain underexplored. We introduce the superfast cosine and sine transforms (SFCT and SFST), extending the TT spectral framework to homogeneous Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions, respectively. Building on a quantum-circuit construction of the discrete cosine and sine transforms, we derive both transforms from a shared TT operator representation and prove that their TT ranks are bounded by $6r_S$, independently of the discretization order, where $r_S$ is the rank of the SFFT at the prescribed accuracy. The measured ranks plateau near 32 for grid sizes up to $2^{26}$ points. For Rayleigh-B\'enard convection, spectral pressure projection achieves up to a 7-fold speedup in the Poisson solve relative to a preconditioned physical-space TT solver while maintaining comparable accuracy. Three-dimensional computational homogenization achieves a 2-6-fold speedup and a 4-7-fold reduction in memory consumption compared with the existing TT-based approach. The results establish an efficient TT framework for spectral PDE solvers with non-periodic boundary conditions.
item.dc:creator: Sascha H. Hauck, Nis-Luca van H\"ulst, Matthias Kabel, Dieter Jaksch, Nicolas R. Gauger

item.title: Uniform Maximum Projection Designs for Computer Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2603.19778v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Space-filling experimental designs are widely used in engineering computer experiments, where only a limited number of expensive model evaluations can be afforded. Distance-based designs such as Maximin or Minimax ensure global space-filling, while Latin hypercube sampling enforces uniform one-dimensional projections, yet neither guarantees uniformity in lowdimensional subspaces. Maximum Projection (MaxPro) designs were introduced to improve uniformity in low-dimensional subspaces, yet their original formulation relies on the Euclidean distance and may induce systematic density distortions in bounded domains. We demonstrate that the standard MaxPro criterion leads to statistically non-uniform sampling, resulting in undersampling of corner regions and biased Monte Carlo estimates. To remedy this issue, we introduce a periodic variant of the criterion, termed Uniform Maximum Projection (uMaxPro), in which the Euclidean metric is replaced by a periodic distance based on the minimum image convention. The proposed uMaxPro designs preserve the projection-aware structure of MaxPro while achieving statistical uniformity of the design-generation mechanism. Numerical experiments show unbiased Monte Carlo integration with reduced variance, excellent subspace projection performance, and competitive discrepancy properties. The methodology is further validated on benchmark engineering problems, including a meso-scale finite element model of concrete, demonstrating improved accuracy in surrogate modeling and probabilistic estimation. The resulting criterion provides a simple and computationally efficient modification of MaxPro that enhances its robustness for nonadaptive computer experiments. The construction algorithm, open-source implementation, and reproducible optimized designs are provided to facilitate practical adoption of the method.
item.dc:creator: Miroslav Vo\v{r}echovsk\'y, Jan Ma\v{s}ek

item.title: Formulation-dependent linearized buckling of stiffened shell panels: role of the stress stiffness operator
item.description: arXiv:2609.22656v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Linearized buckling loads of stiffened panels can diverge across commercial shell formulations because six-degree-of-freedom elements treat drilling rotations and director kinematics differently in the stress stiffness operator. We derive three analytical stress stiffness operators (membrane-only, uncoupled rotational-block, and shear-coupled full second-variation forms), verified against an exact second-difference energy identity. Using direct matrix extraction in ANSYS (SHELL181, SHELL281) and modal and strain-energy benchmarks in Abaqus (S4, S8R), we classify these commercial elements across twelve configurations. On the finest cantilevered shear-panel mesh (in-plane bending and shear), the SHELL181 perturbation and classic procedures predict load factors 11.3% and 28.5% above an independent 3D continuum reference. By contrast, Abaqus S4 and ANSYS SHELL281 lie 5.2% and 5.8% below this reference and remain indistinguishable from the analytical full form within the junction-idealization uncertainty, while Abaqus S8R lies 20.1% below the reference. The tested cases indicate that substantial divergence occurs only when non-coplanar junctions carry pre-stress bending or transverse shear and the buckling mode involves junction drilling rotations. Under pure axial compression or uniform membrane shear flow, the analytical operators coincide and within-element procedures agree within 0.06%. Because buckling under in-plane bending and shear is formulation-dependent, stability design and layout optimization of built-up panels require cross-verification across shell elements or continuum models.
item.dc:creator: Lifeng Wang, Zhongli Qiu, Xuanhao Cheng, Run Du, Wenming Cheng, Min Xie, Xiong Rao

item.title: MiDShip: Multimodal Dataset of Ship Cargo Hold Structures for Engineering Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.02214v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ship structures govern a vessel's strength, safety, and manufacturability. Their design is governed by classification-society rules comprising hundreds of requirements, making the design process complex and highly iterative. However, data-driven structural design is limited by the lack of large, structured datasets that connect design geometry with structural geometric measures and rule-based constraints. This paper presents MiDShip, a multimodal dataset of 12,753 synthetically generated cargo-hold structural designs for machine learning and optimization. It contains 6,020 randomly generated designs, 496 designs produced by a stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD)-inspired procedure, and 6,237 designs produced by an equation-informed repair procedure. Each retained design includes a parametric vector, full 3D geometries and simplified geometries formatted for finite-element analysis (FEA) meshing, engineering drawings and corresponding annotated versions, a bill of materials, and structural geometric measures. The dataset also includes twenty-five constraints formulated from classification society rules for stiffener spacing, thickness, and section modulus requirements. Full-vessel loading, buckling, fatigue, and ice-class checks are outside the present scope. The primary contribution is the dataset and codebase, two design-generation studies demonstrate their use rather than introduce new optimization algorithms. MiDShip supports future research in machine learning, generative design, and automated rule-based evaluation for ship structures.
item.dc:creator: Noah J. Bagazinski, Md. Ferdous Alam, Jaya Manideep Rebbagondla, Faez Ahmed

item.title: Winding-Pack Quench Simulation of Stellarator Coils: Hydraulic Field-Network Coupling and Transverse Heat Conduction in OPENSC$^2$
item.description: arXiv:2611.08084v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quench propagation in cable-in-conduit conductors is thermo-hydraulically driven, yet a standalone 1D model treats a conductor as one straight adiabatic cable with prescribed pressure and mass-flow boundaries, so secondary quenches and flow redistribution between windings cannot be resolved without coupling to further, so far proprietary, codes. We extend the open-source code OPENSC$^2$ with transverse heat conduction between turns, a 3D field resolving the current-sharing temperature, induced losses, and a lumped hydraulic network coupled to the conductors by a mass-flow formulation. Compared to the 2006 W7-X coil tests, it predicts the quench site and cuts the outlet-temperature overestimation from 55 K to 25 K. The identified mechanisms indicate that the position of the helium inlets and outlets relative to the field, the hydraulic interconnection of the windings, the turn insulation and the current dump should be considered together in the quench design of future stellarator coils.
item.dc:creator: Laura A. M. D'Angelo, Felix Warmer

item.title: Certificate-Based Verification of Pulsed Field Ablation Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.18148v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Computational models of cardiac pulsed field ablation predict the lesion as the tissue where the electric field exceeds a lethal threshold. Their numerical error is rarely bounded, and automated pipelines increasingly run them without an expert checking each result. To verify each run, we separate the question "was the stated model solved correctly?" from the solver that answers it. An untrusted solver returns its answer with a certificate, which consists of a potential with the correct electrode and ground values and an exactly charge-conserving current. A small independent checker verifies the certificate against a written specification of the physics. Using the Prager-Synge hypercircle theorem evaluated in ball arithmetic, it turns the certificate into guaranteed two-sided bounds on the impedance and on the root-mean-square field of every tile of a lesion map, also over a range of blood/tissue conductivity ratios. The bounds cover numerical error only; whether the model describes tissue is a question of validation. A vectorized version of the checker takes about a tenth of our solver's time. For a focal electrode in contact, the tile-resolved depth at 1000 V and 700 V/cm is proven to lie in 3.50-3.75 mm for every ratio from 1.7 to 3.75. For a bipolar catheter, certified depths overlap published in-vivo depths. Where they differ from a published reference model, the certificates prove that the difference is not our numerical error. We compare the certificate with a grid convergence study on the same solver. On graded grids, the study is sharper for local fields but remains an estimate. On uniform grids, it fails to converge at the electrode edge, where the certificate still gives a valid bracket. Solvers that deliberately solve equations other than the specified ones pass the grid convergence study, but the certificates refute the impedances they report or leave them unsupported.
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos Dovelos

item.title: A Fast and Accurate Fourier Neural Operator-Based Surrogate for Melt-Pool Prediction in Laser Processing
item.description: arXiv:2602.06241v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-fidelity simulations of laser welding capture complex thermo-fluid phenomena, including phase change, free-surface deformation, and keyhole dynamics, but their computational cost limits large-scale process exploration and real-time use. We present the Laser Processing Fourier Neural Operator (LP-FNO), a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO)-based surrogate model that learns the parametric solution operator of laser processing from multiphysics simulations generated with FLOW-3D WELD. Through a reformulation of the transient problem in a reference frame moving with the laser and the application of temporal averaging, the system is recast into a quasi-steady setting suitable for operator learning, even in the stable keyhole welding regime. LP-FNO maps process parameters to three-dimensional temperature fields and melt-pool boundaries across a broad process window spanning conduction and keyhole regimes using the normalized enthalpy formulation. The model achieves an average temperature relative error of approximately 2.5% and intersection-over-union scores for melt-pool segmentation above 0.9. Compared with a fully connected coordinate network, U-Net, and DeepONet, LP-FNO provides the strongest overall accuracy-efficiency trade-off, while retaining the resolution-invariant evaluation capability characteristic of FNOs. We demonstrate that an LP-FNO model trained on coarse-resolution data can be evaluated on finer grids, yielding accurate super-resolved predictions in mesh-converged conduction regimes, whereas discrepancies in keyhole regimes reflect unresolved dynamics in the coarse-mesh training data. LP-FNO thus provides an efficient surrogate modeling framework for laser welding, predicting full three-dimensional fields and phase interfaces over wide parameter ranges in just tens of milliseconds, up to a hundred thousand times faster than finite-volume multiphysics simulations.
item.dc:creator: Alix Benoit (Empa), Toni Ivas (Empa), Mateusz Papierz (Terra Quantum AG), Asel Sagingalieva (Terra Quantum AG), Alexey Melnikov (Terra Quantum AG), Elia Iseli (Empa)

item.title: Fairness of Explanations in Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Unifying Framework, Axioms, and Future Direction toward Responsible AI
item.description: arXiv:2605.09852v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine learning algorithms are being used in high-stakes decisions, including those in criminal justice, healthcare, credit, and employment. The research community has responded with two largely independent research fields: \emph{algorithmic fairness}, which targets equitable outcomes, and \emph{explainable AI} (XAI), which targets interpretable reasoning. This survey identifies and maps a novel blind spot at their intersection, which is a model that can satisfy every standard fairness criterion in its outputs while being profoundly unfair in its \emph{reasoning process}. We refer to this as the procedural bias, and mitigating it requires treating the fairness of explanations as a distinct object of scientific study. To our knowledge, we provide the first unified theoretical and literature review of this emerging field and elucidate the drawbacks of post-hoc explainers in certifying explanation fairness. Our central contribution is a \emph{conditional invariance framework} formalizing explanation fairness as the requirement that explanations should be indifferent regardless of the protected attributes $ P(E(X) \in \cdot \mid X_\text{rel} = x_\text{rel},\, A = a) = P(E(X) \in \cdot \mid X_\text{rel} = x_\text{rel},\, A = b)$ for all task-relevant $x$, a single principle from which all existing explanation fairness metrics emerge as partial operationalizations. We introduce a seven-dimensional taxonomy, identify three generative mechanisms of explanation inequity (representation-driven, explanation-model mismatch, actionability-driven), and propose a canonical six-step evaluation workflow for operationalizing explanation fairness audits in practice.
item.dc:creator: Gideon Popoola, John Sheppard

item.title: How Attackers Launder Funds through Mixers: Characterization and Detection on Ethereum
item.description: arXiv:2609.27807v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mixers protect privacy by concealing deposit--withdrawal links, but are also abused to launder illicit funds. Existing anti-money laundering studies do not specifically target mixer laundering, while mixer research focuses on deanonymization rather than identifying laundering-related transactions. Public reports remain fragmented, leaving no public case-level dataset for systematic measurement and detection. To fill this void, this paper presents the first comprehensive study of mixer laundering on Ethereum. We first construct \textsc{MixLaunder}, the first public case-level dataset of mixer laundering. It covers 27 cases involving Tornado Cash and Railgun from 2020 to 2025 and labels 9,300 laundering-related transactions with case identities and observable upstream and downstream fund flows, including deposits totaling approximately \$1.1 billion. By comparing these transactions with background mixer usage, we identify five common strategies, showing that laundering evidence spans complementary behavioral and fund-flow contexts, while same-case activity is locally tight but weakly connected across bursts. Our analysis further reveals coverage gaps in mixer-side risk screening and representative deanonymization heuristics. Guided by these findings, we develop \textsc{MixGuard}, which combines tri-view representation learning with two-stage grouping for transaction-level detection and case-aware grouping. Under strict case-level holdout evaluation, \textsc{MixGuard} outperforms representative baselines, achieving 97.89\% detection precision and 98.73\% group purity, while its top ten groups cover 95.09\% of each case's transactions on average.
item.dc:creator: Qishuang Fu, Hang Zheng, Xihan Xiong, Joseph K. Liu, Yixin Liu, Shirui Pan, Qin Wang, Weiqing Wang, Zhipeng Wang, Tsz Hon Yuen
